extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of literature, poets, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for understanding, evaluating, or producing poetry and fine art according to Aristotelian aesthetics (focus on imitation, form, and poetic truth). Useful for literary criticism, creative-writing, and aesthetic theory discussions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as the essence of poetry
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry’s essence lies in the ‘imitation’ (mimesis) of the idea rather than in mere versification; artistic imitation (in the aesthetic sense) is what makes a work poetic, and this can occur in prose as well as verse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text argues for widening the meaning of ‘poet’ to include any writer whose work is an ‘imitation’ in the aesthetic sense (examples: Sophron’s mimes, Xenarchus, Plato’s dialogues). Versification is not the defining criterion — the central question is whether the work imitates life/idea. Avoid equating poetry solely with metre or verse; assess whether the work realizes an imitative artistic idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Metre and melody are subordinate ('seasoning') not essence
rubrics_metrics.description: Metre and melody (rhythmical sound) are described as a ‘seasoning’ or embellishment of language, not the fundamental constituent of poetry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that rhythm and music add charm and can be particularly important in performance-oriented cultures, but they should be treated as auxiliary qualities. Works without metre can still be fully poetic; conversely versifying alone does not guarantee poetry (cf. ‘one may be a poet without versing, and a versifier without poetry’). Evaluate sound and metre as contributors to effect rather than primary determinants of poetic status.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetry expresses the universal, not the particular
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetry ‘expresses most adequately the universal element in human nature and in life’ — it relates ‘what may happen’ (the general, the possible) rather than merely ‘what has happened’ (particular factual events).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging poetic work, prefer readings that reveal universal truths, typical human possibilities, or generalized human types over those that merely chronicle particulars. Distinguish poetic representation from historiography: a poet’s subject is the universal (ta kata_soros) while the historian’s is the particular (ta kata_pragmata). Use this to assess whether a piece attains poetic scope or remains documentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot and action should exhibit probability or necessity (internal causal coherence)
rubrics_metrics.description: A poem/drama must link events in a ‘probable or necessary sequence’ — the internal causal structure should be rigorous, not merely chronological aggregation of incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate plots according to the logical/causal relations among events: do incidents follow from character and prior action by probability or necessity? Avoid accepting mere succession of episodes without causal or probable connection. The rule of probability is not narrow verisimilitude to daily life but internal coherence appropriate to the work’s kinds of characters and actions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as idealisation — art reveals the universal ‘form’ (eidos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art ‘eliminates what is transient and particular and reveals the permanent and essential features’ — it discovers and expresses the ‘form’ toward which objects tend, producing an idealised representation that surpasses the actual.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the work abstracts and purifies particulars into a coherent, ideal type: does it present an intensified, clarified version of human life that captures essential patterns? The artist’s task is to stamp matter with the universal form and harmonise elements into an ideal unity, not to produce slavish copies of appearances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Harmonisation and unity of parts toward a whole
rubrics_metrics.description: The artist must harmonise many elements into an ‘ideal unity of type’; the perfection of art depends on parts co-operating for the good of the whole and on proportion and order.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge structural unity and proportion: do characters, incidents, imagery, and language cohere into an organic whole with interdependent parts? Look for evidence that the creator selected, combined, retrenched, and harmonised elements to express one unified idea or type rather than leaving a disjointed assemblage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Poetic truth: what may happen vs. what did happen
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic truth is concerned with possibility and the general laws of human action (what may happen according to probability or necessity) rather than factual reportage of particular events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing credibility or 'truth' in a poem/fiction, weigh whether it captures believable possibilities and general human truths (moral/psychological plausibility) rather than literal factual accuracy. This defends departures from everyday likelihood when they serve the expression of universal meanings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art is a completion of nature but distinct from useful arts
rubrics_metrics.description: Fine art completes and idealises what nature attempts but does not accomplish; unlike useful arts (which cooperate with nature to achieve practical ends), fine art aims at revealing the ideal rather than serving utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate aims when evaluating works: does the piece pursue aesthetic revelation and ideal completion rather than practical function? Treat signs of purposive idealising as marks of fine art, not as mere functional design. Avoid conflating technical utility with aesthetic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Depth of insight (philosophic knowledge) vs. mere surface imitation
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere surface imitation that copies appearances is inferior to art that grasps and expresses the universal idea; poets limited to narrow experience cannot fully reach the philosophical insight necessary for the highest art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the work’s epistemic depth: does it show an inward comprehension of human motives and universal patterns, or only superficial depiction? Value works that transform experience into insight — look for evidence of reflective understanding beyond anecdotal or merely picturesque description.

rubrics_metrics.name: ‘Embellished language’ and spectacle are auxiliary elements in tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements like ‘embellished language’ (which includes metre and melody) and spectacle (scenery, spectacular effects) are included among constituents of tragedy but are subordinate to imitation and the work’s internal structure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating dramatic works, weigh verbal embellishment and spectacle as supporting devices. Strong tragedy rests on plot, character, and the imitation of universal actions; evaluate spectacle and ornate language for how well they reinforce the central imitative and structural aims rather than as independent justifications for artistic success.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of arts: imitation as criterion for inclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An art is judged ‘fine’ in Aristotle’s sense when it imitates human life or interprets material objects so as to serve the depiction of spiritual/mental processes; arts lacking this imitative relation (e.g., architecture, in Aristotle’s account) may be excluded from fine art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the presence or absence of an ‘imitative’ relation to human life as a criterion for grouping or comparing arts. For creative writers, this helps delimit what counts as fine art: does the medium serve imitation of human character/emotion/action, or is its primary function practical or decorative?
